sec.title: Background
sec.p: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) play pivotal roles in innate immunity and contribute to the advancement of lung cancer. We aimed to identify novel TAM-related biomarkers and significance of macrophage infiltration in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) through an integrative analysis of single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. To describe the cell atlas and construct a novel prognostic signature in LUAD.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The gene signature linked to TAMs was identified utilizing Scanpy from the scRNA-seq dataset GSE131907. Subsequent analysis involved evaluating the expression levels of these genes, their potential molecular mechanisms, and prognostic significance in LUAD using data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) databases. We also constructed a risk score models through LASSO Cox regression for these genes. The underlying mechanism was further elucidated through the application of GSEA, ESTIMATE, TIDE, and other bioinformatic algorithms.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Single-cell atlas was described by analyze 29 scRNA-seq samples from 19 LUAD patients. The TAMs-related gene signature (TGS) was identified as an independent prognostic factor by LASSO Cox regression analysis using differential expression genes (DEGs) derived from pro- and anti-inflammatory macrophage cells. Risk score model including nine TAMs-related genes (FOSL1, ZNF697, ADM, UBE2S, TICAM1, S100P, BIRC3, TLE1, and DEFB1) were obtained for prognosis construction. Moreover, the risk model underwent additional validation in four external GEO cohorts: GSE31210, GSE72094, GSE26939, and GSE30219. Interestingly, TGS-high tumors revealed enrichments in TGF-β signaling and hypoxia pathways, which shown low immune infiltration and immunosuppression by ESTIMATE and TIDE algorithm. The TGS-high risk group exhibited lower richness and diversity in the T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study introduces a novel TGS score developed through LASSO Cox regression analysis, utilizing DEGs in pro- and anti-inflammatory macrophage cells. High TGS tumors exhibited enrichment in TGF-β signaling and hypoxia pathways, suggesting their potential utility in predicting prognosis and immune responses in patients with LUAD. These results offer promising implications for the development of therapeutic strategies for LUAD.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Lung cancer, a prevalent form of cancer globally, exhibits high rates of incidence and mortality [1–3], non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) represents the primary subtype of this disease, known for its genetic and phenotypic diversity, which poses obstacles to the creation of successful treatment approaches [4, 5]. In clinical settings, tumor mutation burden (TMB) and PD-L1 expression are commonly used as indicators to predict the response to immunotherapy [6–8]. Nonetheless, these biomarkers may not entirely represent the varied tumor microenvironment (TME), and the advantages of immunotherapy remain confined to a subset of lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) patients. Therefore, there is an urgent need to identify novel biomarkers and develop predictive models that can predict both prognosis and therapeutic outcome.

Macrophages are essential elements of the immune system and exert considerable influence on the advancement of NSCLC [9–11]. Prior studies have highlighted the dual role of macrophages within the TME, where they can demonstrate either pro-tumor or anti-tumor activities based on their activation state and phenotype [12]. The polarization of macrophages into M2 or M1 subtypes is governed by several signaling pathways [13–15], including the TGF-β pathways [14, 16]. However, TGF-β signaling has been implicated in fostering tumor growth and metastasis by inducing epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and suppressing anti-tumor immune responses [17–19]. Alveolar macrophages are pivotal in lung immune response, with their inflammatory behavior influenced by the activation of different signaling pathways [20, 21]. The intricate equilibrium between pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory alveolar macrophages holds critical significance for the prognosis of NSCLC. Therefore, comprehending this balance is essential to the development of effective immunotherapies for NSCLC.

Over the last decade, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has been instrumental in revealing the molecular and cellular heterogeneity of NSCLC. It has not only provided insights into immunotherapy but has also identified novel therapeutic targets [22–24]. In the context of NSCLC, scRNA-seq has been utilized to investigate alveolar macrophages, pivotal constituents of the lung’s immune system [25, 26]. These immune cells intricately contribute to the tumor microenvironment, shaping anti-tumor immune responses and impacting disease progression. By characterizing the transcriptional landscape of alveolar macrophages in NSCLC patients, researchers have been able to identify distinct subpopulations and functional states, shedding light on the mechanisms underlying TAM behavior [27]. In particular, the analysis of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory responses of alveolar macrophages in NSCLC has been a focal point of intense research due to its potential impact on prognosis and treatment. The TGF-β pathways have been shown to be dysregulated in NSCLC and are important in regulating the immune response. This dysregulation may contribute to the pro-inflammatory response observed in alveolar macrophages, it may also promote tumor growth and metastasis [28]. This information can be used to evaluate prognosis and develop targeted therapies that harness the immune system to combat cancer. As scRNA-seq advances our comprehension of the intricate interplay between alveolar macrophages and NSCLC, it offers the potential to improve patient outcomes and personalize treatment strategies.

Prior research has demonstrated that analyzing gene expression signatures deprived from the molecular features of immune cells obtained from scRNA-seq data can serve as an effective method for forecasting the prognosis of cancer patients and their reaction to immunotherapy [29, 30]. In this study, an in-depth analysis of scRNA-seq data from LUAD was conducted to unravel the molecular characteristics of macrophage cells and identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory alveolar macrophage cells. Furthermore, a TAMs-related gene signature (TGS) was developed via bulk RNA-seq analysis to assess the prognostic implications within the TCGA-LUAD cohort. The predictive efficacy of the TGS was subsequently confirmed across four distinct cohorts sourced from the GEO database, with additional exploration into the correlation between the TGS and immunotherapy response in LUAD.

sec.title: Landscape of cellular atlas in lung cancer
sec.p: To characterize the detailed cellular heterogeneity in the TME of NSCLC samples, we collected and reanalyzed scRNA-seq dataset of GSE131907 [25], which including 19 patients (Fig. S1A) with primary lung tumors (tLung), distant normal lung tissues (nLung), normal lymph nodes (nLN), and metastatic lymph nodes (mLN). We performed principal component analysis (PCA, n_comps = 50) and clustered the neighborhood graph (n_neighbors = 10) using the highly variable genes to reduce the dimensionality, subsequently, a total of 143,158 cells were obtained and clustered into eight major cell subsets (Fig. 1A). As expected, all these major cell lineages showed a good consistency among the different samples with canonical marker gene expression (Fig. S1B and S1C). While T cells, B cells, Plasma B cells, epithelial cells, fibroblasts cells, endothelial cells, myeloid cells, and NK cells were significantly characterized by specific high expression of CD3D, MS4A1, MZB1, EPCAM, DCN, CLDN5, LYZ, and NKG7, respectively (Fig. 1B). Interestingly, expression of discriminating canonical marker genes was enriched in each cell cluster, which indicates that they have similar gene expression patterns to distinguish from different cell lineages (Fig. 1C). Taken together, we described the landscapes of cell clusters across 19 LUAD patients for further analysis.

caption.p: Comprehensive analysis of LUAD single cell atlas. A UMAP plots of major cell lineages. B Dot plot of corresponding canonical marker genes, which represented each cell lineage. C Heatmap of three canonical marker genes in each major cell lineage

sec.title: Characterization of different myeloid cell clusters in LUAD
sec.p: Myeloid cell clusters are critical players in regulate inflammation and maintenance of lung homeostasis. After strict quality control and filtration, we found a total of 34,770 myeloid cells these myeloid cells were divided into macrophages, dendritic cells (DCs), plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), monocytes, and mast cells based on canonical cell markers (Fig. 2A). We observed 24,828 cells were enrichment of MARCO, APOE, and FN1, suggesting that this subset may be an accurate macrophages cluster (Fig. S2A). Our data also indicated that most cell markers were uniquely expressed in each cell subset (Fig. S2B and S2C).

caption.p: Expression genes of myeloid cell clusters in LUAD patients. A UMAP plot of myeloid cells, colored by five cell clusters. B UMAP plot of 24,828 macrophage cells, colored by three cell types. C Proportions (left) and cell number (right) of three major macrophage cell types across nLung, tLung, nLN, and mLN tissues. D UMAP plot of 11,970 alveolar macrophages cells, colored by three cell sub-clusters. E Dot plot of three represented expressed genes in pro-inflammatory, anti-inflammatory, and unclear cell clusters

sec.p: We performed unsupervised graph-based clustering by CellTypist on macrophages and then identified three subsets, including alveolar macrophages (alveolar Mφ), Monocyte-derived macrophages (Monocyte-derived Mφ), and interstitial macrophages perivascular (interstitial Mφ perivascular) (Fig. 2B). Of note, all these cell subtypes were shared among nLung, tLung, nLN, and mLN patients, although with different proportions (Fig. 2C). Interestingly, alveolar Mφ exhibited a much higher proportion in nLung, also with more cell numbers than those of other cell subtypes (Fig. 2C). In addition, 11,970 alveolar Mφ were re-analyzed by UMAP and identified as different functional subsets (Fig. 2D). For example, pro-inflammatory alveolar Mφ were expressed IL1B [31], KDM6B, and CCL20. By contrast, TREM2 [32, 33], POLR3, and IFI6 were expressed in anti-inflammatory alveolar Mφ. The function of remaining cluster was unclear and defined (Fig. 2E).

sec.title: Construction of the prognostic signature based on alveolar macrophage genes
sec.p: To identify functional differences in alveolar macrophage (Mφ) cell clusters, we performed Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney tests between pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory alveolar Mφ cell clusters to calculate the DEGs. We identified 422 up-regulated genes and 71 down-regulated genes (Fig. 3A). To construct a prognostic signature based on these DEGs, the TCGA-LUAD cohort was employed as the training set, and a LASSO Cox proportional hazards regression analysis was conducted. Finally, only 9 most predictive genes were selected for risk prognostic model. Risk score = (0.091 × FOSL1 expression) + (0.075 × ZNF697 expression) + (0.029 × ADM expression) + (0.120 × UBE2S expression) + (0.005 × TICAM1 expression) + (0.042 × S100P expression) + (0.020 × BIRC3 expression) + (0.294 × TLE1 expression) + (0.012 × DEFB1 expression) (Fig. 3B). Therefore, we defined a novel prognostic gene signature for further analysis.

caption.p: Macrophage gene expression landscape and survival outcomes. A Volcano plot for expression of differentially expressed genes between pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cells. B Forest plots show HRs (pink circle) and 95% confidence intervals (horizontal ranges) derived from cox regression survival analyses for overall survival of nine macrophage signature genes

sec.p: The cutoff for the risk score was determined as 3.1045 according to the descending order of risk scores, segregating the cohort into low-risk (n = 330, two thirds of all samples) and high-risk (n = 165, one third of all samples) groups. The distribution of risk scores, survival status and expression profiling were showed (Fig. 4A), indicating increased mortality and higher expression in high-risk groups. KM analysis was performed to demonstrate that high-risk patients with significantly poor overall survival (OS) than low-risk patients (Fig. 4B, HR = 2.35, p < 0.001). The accuracy of the prognostic model based on risk scores was assessed through time-dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis for OS. The analysis yielded AUC values for 1, 3, and 5 years at 0.721, 0.716, and 0.675, respectively (Fig. 4C). The investigation proceeded to determine if a high-risk designation acts as an independent prognostic marker for OS. Conducting a multivariate Cox proportional hazards analysis that incorporated variables such as gender, age, tumor stage, and the calculated risk score, it was found that the risk score independently predicts OS outcomes in the TCGA-LUAD dataset (p < 0.001, Fig. 4D). Overall, these findings suggest that the risk score is a reliable predictor of the prognosis of LUAD patients, regardless of their age, gender, or tumor stage.

caption.p: Construction of prognostic model with macrophage signature genes in the TCGA-LUAD cohort. A The distribution of risk score (top), survival status (middle), and expression (bottom) of the identified nine macrophage cell marker genes. B Kaplan–Meier curves of survival analysis compared the overall survival of LUAD patients between TGS-high and TGS-low groups. C ROC curves of the TGS for predicting the risk of death at 1, 3, and 5 years. D Forest plot representation of multivariate model with adjustment for confounding factors in TCGA-LUAD cohort

sec.title: Validation of the TGS in different independent cohorts
sec.p: In this study, four independent GEO cohorts (GSE31210, GSE72094, GSE26939, and GSE30219) were included to validate the robustness of the TGS. Risk scores were calculated for each patient in the specified cohorts using the established formula. Patients were then classified into high-risk and low-risk categories based on their risk scores, with the top one-third designated as high-risk and the remaining two-thirds as low-risk. Finally, the KM analyses conducted across all four GEO independent cohorts indicated that individuals in the high-risk category experienced significantly worse outcomes compared to those in the low-risk group. GEO datasets, including GSE31210 (Fig. 5A, HR: 1.98, 95% CI 1.09–3.59, p = 0.039), GSE72094 (Fig. 5B, HR: 2.14, 95% CI 1.52–3.02, p < 0.0001), GSE26939 (Fig. 5C, HR: 1.63, 95% CI 1.05–2.54, p = 0.049), and GSE30219 (Fig. 5D, HR: 1.35, 95% CI 1.06–1.73, p = 0.035). Together, these findings collectively underscore the prognostic utility of the TGS risk score in predicting outcomes for patients with LUAD.

caption.p: Validation of the TGS in four independent GEO cohorts. A GSE31210 (n = 226). B GSE30219 (n = 83). C GSE37745 (n = 106). D GSE50081 (n = 127)

sec.title: Functional enrichment analysis of the TGS related signature genes
sec.p: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was further performed to investigate significant enrichment pathway related to TGS. Using hallmark gene sets (c2.cp.v7.4.symbols.gmt) as a reference, we found the high-risk group to be enriched in TGF-β signaling pathway (Fig. 6A). GSEA analysis further indicated that DEGs related to TGS-high group were also significantly enriched in TGF-β signaling pathway (Fig. 6B, NES = 2.824, p = 5.16e-11). Furthermore, gene set variation analysis (GSVA) demonstrated the functional activity within the TGS risk score group, revealing increased pathway activity in the Pan-F-TBRS (Fig. 6C, p = 0.003) and the hypoxia signature (Fig. 6D, p = 1.2e−09). These results enlightening us to consider the potential mechanism of TGS-high group, which was enriched immunosuppression and low immune infiltration. Therefore, we next to explore the immune infiltration differences between TGS-high and TGS-low groups.

caption.p: Function analysis between TGS-high and TGS-low groups. A Function enrichment of TGS-high and TGS-low groups in TCGA-LUAD cohort. B GSEA analysis of hallmark TGF-β signaling pathway. GSVA activity of Pan-F-TBRS (C) and hallmark hypoxia (D) pathway

sec.title: Immune infiltration of the TGS groups
sec.p: To investigate the properties and functions of TGS-high and TGS-low groups, we evaluated the correlation between TGS and immune cell infiltration in TCGA-LUAD patients. Using the ESTIMATE algorithm [34], we observed that TGS-high patients had lower stromal score (Fig. 7A, p = 0.049), immune score (Fig. 7B, p = 0.0012), ESTIMATE score (Fig. S3A, p = 0.0047), and higher tumor purity (Fig. S3B, p = 0.047) than TGS-low patients, suggesting that the TGS risk score was negatively correlated with the degree of immune cell infiltration. Furthermore, the tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion (TIDE) algorithm was applied to predict the likelihood of immune escape in the TCGA-LUAD cohort [35]. The TIDE analysis indicated that TGS-high patients had a higher exclusion score (Fig. 7C, p = 8.6e−09) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) score (Fig. 7D, p < 2.22e−16) using gene signatures of immune evasion through T cell exclusion. Overall, these results indicate that the TGS-high group was negatively correlated with the tumor and may be a general regulator of immune evasion.

caption.p: The association between TGS and immune cell infiltration in the TME, and its role in predicting immunotherapy benefits. Differences among stromal score (A), immune score (B) between TGS-high and TGS-low groups. TIDE analysis in TGS-high and TGS-low groups, including exclusion score (C) and MDSC score (D). TCR richness (A) and TCR diversity (B) between TGS-high and TGS-low groups

sec.title: Prediction of immunotherapy benefits in LUAD Patients
sec.p: T cells are pivotal in mediating the immune response against tumors, thereby enhancing the specificity and efficacy of immunotherapy. Prior investigations have established that T cells, when genetically modified to express specific T cell receptors (TCRs) targeting cancer antigens, enhance the recognition of antigens presented by the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC). TCR profiling has emerged as a credible biomarker for assessing the anti-tumor immune response [36–38]. In our analysis, we scrutinized TCR diversity utilizing a TCR repertoire database [39, 40], comparing TGS-high and TGS-low patient groups. Notably, we discovered a significant reduction in both TCR richness (Fig. 7E, p = 0.0033) and Shannon diversity index (Fig. 7F, p = 0.0012) in the TGS-high group compared to the TGS-low group, suggesting that lower TGS scores might predict a better response to immunotherapy.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Exploring the tumor microenvironment of LUAD is a productive and efficient method to decode molecular characteristics and mechanisms for clinical diagnostics and prognosis studies. Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis has unveiled significant heterogeneity among macrophages in NSCLC, both within and between tumors [25]. For instance, certain macrophages exhibit elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, while others display heightened levels of anti-inflammatory cytokines. Moreover, some macrophages are actively phagocytosing tumor cells, while others are predominantly inactive. These differences in macrophage phenotype and function may have significant implications for prognosis and therapy response. Identifying patients who will benefit from immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy remains a primary challenge in treating NSCLC [41]. While a subset of NSCLC patients with high levels of PD-L1 expression and/or TMB has demonstrated promise in responding to immunotherapy [42]. Employing single-cell analysis may aid in discovering additional biomarkers for predicting responses to immunotherapy. Beyond the identification of new biomarkers, single-cell analysis is pivotal in unraveling the mechanisms behind the development of resistance to immunotherapy. Recent study has demonstrated that tumor cells may elude immune surveillance by undergoing epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), which enables them to avoid detection by T cells. TGF-β signaling has been associated with EMT induction [43, 44], and targeting this pathway may could improve the efficacy of immunotherapy [45]. Overall, the utilization of single-cell analysis has the capacity to greatly improve our understanding of the molecular and cellular diversity present in NSCLC, and may lead to the discovery of novel therapeutic targets for the treatment of lung cancer. The intricate interplay between macrophages, TGF-β signaling, and the immune system in NSCLC emphasizes the importance of investigating this disease at the individual cell level. Through the analysis of NSCLC heterogeneity and identification of new biomarkers and treatment targets, there is potential to improve the outcomes for patients affected by this devastating disease.

This study presents a new prognostic prediction model utilizing a gene signature associated with TAMs for patients with LUAD in the TCGA database, subsequently validated in four separate cohorts from the GEO dataset.

The TGS included nine alveolar macrophage marker genes: FOSL1, ZNF697, ADM, UBE2S, TICAM1, S100P, BIRC3, TLE1, and DEFB1, most of which are linked to LUAD prognosis or macrophage activity. FOSL1, a key transcription factor, regulates differentiation, proliferation, and survival. Its elevated expression is associated with poor outcomes in KRAS-mutant LUAD and promotes an immunosuppressive macrophage phenotype that drives tumor progression [46, 47]. ZNF697 is involved in transcription regulation, with GWAS studies suggesting it may predict IFNβ therapy response in multiple sclerosis [48, 49]. ADM regulates hormone secretion, angiogenesis, and antimicrobial activity, playing a role in ILD prognosis and hypoxia-induced ILC2 activation [50–52]. UBE2S is overexpressed in lung cancer and correlates with tumor progression and poor prognosis in NSCLC [53, 54]. TICAM1, involved in TLR signaling, contributes to cancer cell migration and invasion, suggesting autophagy inhibition as a potential therapeutic approach [55]. S100P, a member of the S100 protein family, promotes cancer metastasis, and its knockdown reduces cell migration in invasive NSCLC cells [56, 57]. BIRC3, an inhibitor of apoptosis, has been linked to cisplatin resistance and tumor infiltration in lung cancer [58, 59]. TLE1 promotes EMT and NF-κB signaling and is part of a B cell-specific signature used to predict prognosis and immunotherapy response in LUAD [60–62]. DEFB1, involved in the innate immune response, shows potential as a biomarker for immunotherapy [63, 64]. The TGS Prognostic Signature reliably predicts patient prognosis in both the training and validation cohorts. To gain further insight into the mechanism of TGS groups, we conducted GO pathway and GSEA analyses. The TGS-high group exhibited enrichment in TGF-β signaling and hypoxia pathways. Furthermore, we used the ESTIMATE and TIDE algorithms to assess immune infiltration and immunosuppression and found that the TGS-high group exhibited low levels of immune infiltration and immunosuppression. Additionally, analysis of the TCR repertoire’s richness and diversity revealed a negative correlation between inflammatory activity and risk score in the TGS-high risk group.

Despite its significance, this study has limitations that require attention. Firstly, the analysis did not account for the distinct clinical stages of LUAD. Moreover, the candidate genes were restricted to macrophage cell marker genes. It is known that the tumor immune microenvironment is highly spatially heterogeneous, which may limit the prognostic value of the signature. Additionally, the mechanistic analyses in the study were purely descriptive, indicating the need for future research to clarify the mechanisms that link the gene signature to LUAD prognosis. Despite these limitations, the study is a crucial reference for the personalized treatment of LUAD patients, emphasizing the need for further research to improve the clinical utility of the gene signature.

sec.title: Data collection of single cell RNA sequencing and GEO datasets
sec.p: Original scRNA-seq dataset (GSE131907) were collected and reanalyzed [25], which including 19 patients with primary lung tumors (tLung), distant normal lung tissues (nLung), normal lymph nodes (nLN), and metastatic lymph nodes (mLN). Gene expression profiles of LUAD were downloaded from TCGA (https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/). The raw read counts and clinical characteristics of LUAD patients, were obtained from UCSC Xena websites (https://xenabrowser.net/datapages/). Several independent cohorts used for model validation were downloaded from NCBI GEO database, including GSE31210 (n = 226), GSE72094 (n = 398), GSE26939 (n = 114), and GSE30219 (n = 289).

sec.title: Single cell clustering and cell type annotation
sec.p: The expression matrix from single cell dataset was individually imported to Scanpy (version 1.9.1) for further analysis. Principal component analysis (PCA, parameters: n_comps = 50) was performed with ‘sc.tl.pca’, and the neighborhood graph (parameters: n_neighbors = 10) were clustered with ‘sc.pp.neighbors’. Highly variable genes were calculated to reduce the dimensionality, and cell clusters were then identified with Louvain algorithm by “sc.tl.louvain” module (parameters: resolution = 0.4). Subsequently, cell clusters was visualized through uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) module “sc.pl.umap”. The annotation of each cell clusters was defined by the expression of known marker genes with CellTypist (https://github.com/Teichlab/celltypist).

sec.title: Construction and validation of prognostic model
sec.p: A univariate Cox regression analysis was conducted to assess the prognostic significance of pro- and anti-inflammatory alveolar macrophage cell marker genes for OS in TCGA-LUAD patients. Genes with a p value less than 0.01 were identified as prognostic genes. Subsequently, the prognostic genes were evaluated using the LASSO Cox regression method, implemented in the R package “glmnet”. Following the LASSO Cox regression analysis, a risk model was constructed by combing the mRNA expression of the genes with their respective risk coefficients. In conclusion, a total of nine genes were chosen as significant prognostic markers for further investigation. Using a one third cut-off value, the patients were categorized into the TGS-high and TGS-low groups. To confirm the prognostic value of TGS, we employed receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves [65] and utilized the R package “survivalROC” to compute the area under the curve (AUC), which served as an indicator of the TGS model’s accuracy.

sec.title: Survival analysis
sec.p: The prognostic value of TGS-related genes in TCGA-LUAD was analyzed using Kaplan–Meier curves (R packages ‘survival’ and ‘survminer’). The predictive ability of the TGS was validated using four independent GEO datasets.

sec.title: Differentially expressed gene analysis
sec.p: The expression of each gene in each cell cluster was compared to the rest of the cells using the Wilcoxon rank sum test by module “sc.tl.rank_genes_groups”. The up-regulated or down-regulated gene was, defined with a p value less than 0.05, the log (fold change) ≥ 1 or ≤ − 1, respectively.

sec.title: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)
sec.p: GSEA was performed to detect significant enrichment pathways with hallmark gene sets (c2.cp.v7.4.symbols.gmt) from MSigDB (http://software.broadinstitute.org/gsea/msigdb/).

sec.title: Gene set variation analysis (GSVA)
sec.p: GSVA was performed to identify activity of enriched pathway between TGS-high and -low groups. The enrichment scores of the gene sets in each TCGA-LUAD sample were quantified by the ssGSEA algorithm using the R package “GSVA”.

sec.title: Stromal and immune scores from ESTIMATE
sec.p: ESTIMATE algorithm was used to estimate the ratio of immune-stromal components in tumor microenvironment (TME) for each sample. The resultant Stromal Score, Immune Score, ESTIMATE Score, and Tumor Purity provided quantifiable indices representing the respective ratios of stromal and immune components, their aggregate, and the intrinsic tumor purity. Higher values of these scores signify greater relative proportions of the corresponding components within the TME [34].

sec.title: Tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion (TIDE) analysis
sec.p: TIDE algorithm was utilized to predict the potential response to Immune Checkpoint Blockade (ICB) therapy [35]. Higher TIDE scores are associated with reduced efficacy of ICB treatment [66]. Recent studies have reported the usefulness of TIDE in predicting or evaluating the efficacy of ICB therapy [67–69].

sec.title: TCR analysis
sec.p: TCR repertoire analysis has emerged as a valuable biomarker for tumor immune responsiveness. In this study, we analyzed the TCR richness and diversity of each TGS group using the method introduced in a previous study [39].

sec.title: Statistics analysis
sec.p: Statistical significance was determined using a two-tailed Student’s t-test within the R software environment (version v4.0.3). The Cox proportional hazards model was employed for multivariate analysis to ascertain independent predictors of OS in TCGA-LUAD and GEO datasets, utilizing the R packages ‘survival’, ‘survminer’, and ‘forestplot’. The FDR method was applied to adjust the p-values, with significance established at p values or FDR less than 0.05. An adjusted p-value below 0.05 was considered the threshold for significance.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: The scRNA-seq dataset was acquired from the GEO database, specifically under accession number GSE131907. The TCGA-LUAD cohort dataset was downloaded from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA, https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/) portal. Moreover, the validation datasets were acquired from GEO database, including GSE31210, GSE72094, GSE26939, and GSE30219.
